source: Yokohama National University group (2025) Bandit-Based Prompt Design Strategy Selection Improves Prompt Optimizers (OPTS)
finding: Adds explicit strategy choice to the EvoPrompt prompt optimizer. Three selectors: Thompson sampling (TS), uniform (US), and letting the LLM pick (APET). Eleven strategies plus an inaction arm. TS is best on average.
numbers: BBH, 27 tasks, Llama-3-8B-Instruct as solver, GPT-4o mini as prompt designer, population 10, 50 iterations, 3 seeds. All OPTS variants raise EvoPrompt(DE) mean score by about 4.5% to 7.5%. TS beats uniform by about 1.7% and LLM-picks by about 2.7%.
quote: OPTS(APET) is inferior to OPTS(US), implying that LLMs have an incorrect bias in selecting prompt design strategies.
limits: Gains are task-dependent. OPTS lowers score on several tasks (the inaction arm limits the loss). Bernoulli reward only. Only EvoPrompt tested. Three seeds, large SDs on some tasks.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that code-side Thompson sampling picks operators better than asking the model, which supports guardrail G5 and the rule that the program chooses the operator.

source: OPTS (2025) Table 3, GPT-4o mini as task solver
finding: With GPT-4o mini as solver on three random BBH tasks, EvoPrompt(DE)-OPTS(TS) is better on all three, with one huge jump and two tiny ones.
numbers: Task 8 (logical deduction five objects): 2.67 (SD 1.43) to 52.33 (SD 11.45). Task 19: 79.17 to 79.43. Task 23: 80.67 to 81.83. Three trials each.
limits: The big jump is from a near-zero baseline (likely a broken baseline prompt), not a general 50% gain. Only three tasks. The headline claim of up to 50% is one task.
agent_relevance: Large reported gains from operator selection can hide a baseline that was broken. Report per task, not just the maximum.

source: OPTS (2025) qualitative analysis of selected strategies
finding: Repeated application of the same strategy (for example chain of thought applied twice to one prompt) helped fold it in better. Found prompts mixed several strategies that plain EvoPrompt did not find.
numbers: No count given; shown as examples (Tables 4 and 5) from one trial.
limits: Anecdotal; one trial shown.
agent_relevance: Bandit arms need not be exclusive; an operator may help more when re-applied. Do not forbid repeats in the schema operator picker.

source: Shi et al. (2024) Efficient Prompt Optimization Through the Lens of Best Arm Identification (TRIPLE), NeurIPS
finding: Frames choosing among candidate prompts as fixed-budget best-arm identification, not regret minimisation. Sequential halving (SH) and continuous rejection (CR) beat uniform allocation and UCB when the evaluation budget is small.
numbers: 30 candidate prompts, budget 150 evaluations (5 per prompt). GPT-3.5: SH +15% and CR +12% over Uniform; +5% and +3% over UCB. Llama2: SH +15%, CR +16% over Uniform; +6%, +7% over UCB.
limits: Gains measured as normalised test accuracy on pools of APE-generated prompts, relative to the baseline's own accuracy. Selection stage only, not generation.
agent_relevance: On small budgets the goal is to pick the best operator, not to maximise cumulative reward. UCB regret logic targets the wrong thing for a short run; use halving or racing.

source: TRIPLE (2024) budget sweep and embedding variants
finding: Advantage of bandit allocation shrinks as budget grows and vanishes when budget is generous. With more prompts than budget, sharing information through prompt embeddings is needed.
numbers: At 10 evaluations per prompt: CR +9.7%, CLST +13.5%, GSE +17.4% over Uniform. At 20 per prompt: about +8% for CLST and GSE. At 30 per prompt: all methods about equal. With 150 prompts and budget 100: CLST and GSE beat BO-EI by 21% and 28% (GPT-3.5) and NeuralUCB by 38% and 45%.
limits: One task family and two LLMs; embeddings assume prompts with similar text perform alike.
agent_relevance: Bandit value is largest exactly in the small-budget regime our agent lives in. When arms outnumber pulls, group operators by type and share statistics.

source: Pryzant et al. (2023) Automatic Prompt Optimization with Gradient Descent and Beam Search (ProTeGi)
finding: Uses bandit selection (UCB, UCB-E, successive rejects, successive halving) to choose which candidate prompts to evaluate. Every bandit selector beat uniform spending of the same query budget. UCB beat successive rejects, contrary to theory.
limits: Differences between bandit variants are 0.01 to 0.04, probably inside noise. Contradicts best-arm-identification theory, and TRIPLE finds the opposite ordering (SH and CR over UCB).
agent_relevance: Any bandit beats uniform; the choice among bandits matters little at this scale. Do not spend design effort on the fanciest algorithm.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS), Sakana AI
finding: Tree search where Thompson sampling decides at each node between generating a new answer (go wider) and refining an existing one (go deeper). UCT cannot be used because new arms are created on the fly. Beats repeated sampling and standard MCTS on code and ML tasks but not on ARC-AGI at 128 samples.
numbers: Budget 128 generations, mean rank over 6 settings: Repeated Sampling 3.5, AB-MCTS-M 2.3, AB-MCTS-A 2.7. ARC-AGI Pass@2: repeated sampling 15.0 (GPT-4o) and 18.6 (DeepSeek-V3), AB-MCTS-M 12.3 and 16.0, AB-MCTS-A 14.0 and 16.6. CodeContest GPT-4o: 40.6 (AB-MCTS-M) vs 37.9 (repeated sampling). LiveCodeBench GPT-4o: 38.9 vs 37.8.
limits: Gains on LiveCodeBench are about 1 point with SD up to 2.4. On ARC-AGI repeated sampling is the best baseline until about 200 to 500 generations.
agent_relevance: The wider-versus-deeper choice is a Thompson-sampling decision that fits our operators (new attempt vs revise). On ARC the plain wide sampler is a strong baseline that bandit search only overtakes at large budgets.

source: AB-MCTS (2025) MLE-Bench and scaling to 512 generations
finding: On three MLE-Bench Kaggle tasks the best baseline changes from task to task, while AB-MCTS-M stays strong on all. On ARC-AGI with DeepSeek-V3, repeated sampling plateaus between 200 and 500 generations while AB-MCTS keeps improving.
numbers: GPT-4o only on MLE-Bench (GPU cost), three competitions. ARC-AGI budget up to 2^9 = 512.
limits: Few tasks. Beta and Gaussian-model variants differ by about 1 point.
agent_relevance: Task-adaptive allocation is the main value: no fixed wide/deep ratio is best everywhere. Supports a state-dependent operator mix instead of a fixed schedule.

source: Sakana AI (2025) ShinkaEvolve: Towards Open-Ended and Sample-Efficient Program Evolution
finding: Evolutionary code search that picks which LLM writes each mutation with a UCB1 bandit. Reward is relative improvement over the parent: exp(max(r - baseline, 0)) - 1, normalised, to favour bold gains over small ones. Ablation: bandit ensemble beats a single LLM and slightly beats a fixed uniform ensemble.
numbers: Circle packing ablation. The figure caption says the bandit 'slightly improves' over uniform; the takeaway text says it 'significantly outperforms'. New state of the art circle packing with 150 samples. About 2.3% gain over ALE-Agent across 10 ALE-Bench tasks.
limits: Ablation on one task; no numbers or error bars in the text read. Caption and takeaway disagree on the size of the bandit effect. Reward shaping is hand designed.
agent_relevance: A working template for a code-side bandit with an improvement-over-parent reward. Expect a small gain over uniform; the larger win is over a single model.

source: Simonides (2026) LLaMEA operator analysis and selection, Leiden University MSc thesis
finding: Tests informed operator selection inside LLaMEA (LLM-written optimisation algorithms). No single prompt operator is best across the search; operator value falls as parent fitness rises. Bandit selectors beat random only slightly and with large run-to-run noise.
numbers: Gemini flash-lite, dimension 5, budget 400 evaluations, 6 runs per method. Mean final fitness: Random 0.8304 (SD 0.0148); UCB 0.8453 (SD 0.0296); SW-UCB-S 0.8417; SW-UCB-M 0.8401; SW-UCB-L 0.8235 (below random); Top3 0.8350; Geometric-S 0.8470.
limits: Master's thesis, not peer reviewed. Gap between UCB and random (0.015) is about one SD; N = 6. The author says the differences are relatively small.
agent_relevance: A sober small-sample result: a bandit over LLM prompt operators gives at best a point-level gain and can lose to random with a bad window. Do not expect more than a modest edge.

source: Simonides (2026) thesis, operator utilisation
finding: Sliding-window UCB with a small window drifts back to near-uniform selection late in the run because it forgets too fast. Plain UCB keeps a clear preference while still exploring.
numbers: Windows 30, 60, 120 tried; selection divergence from uniform measured by total variation distance.
limits: Six runs each; one benchmark (MA-BBOB); one LLM.
agent_relevance: Window size is a real tuning risk. With few pulls (our case) a window forgets everything; prefer discounting, or no window plus change detection tied to a code-visible event.

source: TIDE (2026) Tuning-Integrated Dynamic Evolution for LLM-Based Automated Heuristic Design
finding: Treats the choice of prompting strategy (mutation or crossover type) as a non-stationary bandit with UCB1 (exploration constant sqrt(2)). Reward is relative fitness gain over the current best. Ablating UCB to random selection changes results, but not in the same direction at every size.
numbers: Qwen3-Max, 6 islands, population 8 per island, 800 generations. Ablation relative gaps (%), lower is better, sizes 50/100/200: w/o UCB 5.87, 8.91, 12.64; w/o migration 8.00, 9.97, 10.73; w/o parameter refinement 8.01, 9.74, 10.85. Averaged over 3 runs. Full-model row not captured in the text read.
limits: At size 50 the no-UCB variant is the best of the three ablations; at size 200 it is the worst. Three runs. Full-model row missing from my extraction.
agent_relevance: UCB over prompt strategies is now standard in LLM heuristic design papers, but the ablation shows mixed value by problem size.

source: Deliberate Evolution (2026) agentic symbolic regression with adaptive operators
finding: Four operators (refine, mutate, crossover, regenerate) ordered from exploit to explore. Operator weights are kept per search state, a pair of binary flags: parent rank good or not, region visited often or not. Policy mixes learned weights with a uniform floor. Ablation: fixed Refine or uniform sampling is much worse than the adaptive policy.
numbers: Physics set, Qwen3-4B. NMSE and Acc0.01: full model 4.37e-4 and 15.91%; fixed Refine 8.69e-3 and 9.52%; Uniform 1.02e-2 and 6.82%; without the stagnation monitor 7.69e-4 and 13.64%. Removing tools 2.52e-2 and 4.55%.
limits: Small benchmark: 15.91% vs 6.82% is probably 7 vs 3 of 44 problems (our inference). Single seed shown. Tool removal hurts more than operator selection.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our design: operators chosen by a code-side policy conditioned on a small discrete state, with a stagnation signal. Supports G1 (act on stagnation) and the state-to-operator mapping.

source: CoEvo-AHD (2026) LLM-driven co-evolutionary automated heuristic design
finding: Uses a global UCB1 rule to choose parents for crossover and a local bandit per operator. Low-ranked operators are pruned and their bandit statistics deleted so new LLM-written operators start clean.
numbers: Ablation on TTP50: removing the tool-augmented environment gives 1634.79, about 5.54% lower than the full framework. No bandit-only ablation found in the text read.
limits: Read only the method and part of the ablation text.
agent_relevance: Shows a pattern for operators the LLM invents on the fly: reset statistics when the arm set changes.

source: Sui et al. (2025, ACL Findings 2026) Meta-Reasoner: Dynamic Guidance for Optimized Inference-time Reasoning
finding: A contextual bandit (LinUCB) picks a high-level move each round from a progress report: continue with suggestions, backtrack, restart, try another method. A separate model scores progress as the reward. A dynamic version lets an LLM add new strategies.
numbers: Authors report 9 to 12% higher accuracy and 28 to 35% less inference time than prior methods. Ablation, GPT-4o-mini: Game-of-24 89 full, 85 without progress report, 82 with LLM picking the strategy directly, 4 for plain CoT. TheoremQA 84.13, 79.42, 80.74, 39.46. Gemini-exp-1206: 94, 91, 87, 11.
limits: The collapse (89 to 4) is plain CoT, not a fair no-bandit control. The fair control, LLM picks the strategy directly, costs only 7 points on Game-of-24 and 3.4 on TheoremQA. Training queries: 50 for Game-of-24, 30 each for the others. The reward model is itself an LLM.
agent_relevance: The honest bandit effect over LLM self-selection is a few points. Strategy names like backtrack and restart match our operators. The progress report acts as a state, which is useful, but its reward is a model judgment, which conflicts with G2 and G5.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: LLMs used as bandit agents mostly fail to explore. Of all prompt and model setups tried, only one worked: GPT-4 with chain of thought and a history summary supplied as sufficient statistics (counts and means).
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2; Bernoulli bandit K = 5, gap 0.2 (hard) and K = 4, gap 0.5 (easy); T = 500 rounds, 20 replicates for headline runs, 10 replicates across 10 configurations. GPT-4 basic prompt: suffix failure (never picks the best arm again) in more than 60% of replicates. All but five configurations have at least 15% suffix-failure frequency at T/2.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Few replicates; authors say results are at moderate scale and short horizon. Small arm counts. Older models.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model run its own explore-exploit loop. Code must keep counts and means and make the selection, or give the model only summaries, which fits G1 and G5.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For In-Context Exploration (BanditBench)
finding: Benchmark of natural-language bandits. Giving the LLM UCB-computed values (mean plus bonus) in the prompt helps most. Fine-tuning on UCB trajectories lets a small model beat a larger one. Raw history is weakest.
numbers: Overall win-rate (%) by pairwise t-test, 30 trials per config, 16 MAB and 2 contextual-bandit configs. Table layout was garbled in my extraction, so pairings are my best reading. Gemini-1.5 Flash MAB: raw history 27.5 vs algorithm-guided 50.2; Pro: 39.1 vs 56.4. Contextual bandit Flash: 3.6 vs 60.7; Pro 7.1 vs 25.0. UCB itself 90.6 (Flash set) and 96.4 (Pro set). Fine-tuned Flash with raw history 65.6. Text: few-shot with summary 50.2% vs raw history 27.5%; adding guided values to fine-tuning data in contextual bandits raised win-rate 28.6 to 89.3.
limits: Win-rate hides the size of regret differences. Table pairing uncertain.
agent_relevance: Numbers handed to the model (counts, means, bonus) are worth far more than raw history. UCB beats every LLM variant. Compute the bandit in code and show only the result.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3, PNAS
finding: An older GPT-3 model beat humans on a bandit task but showed no sign of directed exploration (choosing the less-sampled arm for information) in the horizon task.
numbers: Horizon task: mean regret GPT-3 2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26). Long-horizon first-trial regret lower than humans (t(5550) = -4.07, p < .001); final regret difference not significant (t = -0.75). No positive horizon effect in the unequal-information condition, and no reward-difference by horizon interaction.
limits: One 2022 model, text prompts, two-armed bandit with 4 forced trials then 1 or 6 free trials.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that models exploit well but do not explore on purpose, which is the gap a code-side bonus fills.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Exploration-exploitation of LLMs vs humans vs MAB algorithms, with and without reasoning
finding: Compares LLMs, humans and UCB, Thompson, epsilon-greedy on a 2-armed stationary and a 4-armed non-stationary task. Reasoning (chain of thought or reasoning-tuned models) raises directed exploration and cuts regret, reaching human level on the 2-armed task. On the 4-armed task directed exploration stays absent.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-pro, DeepSeek-V3 and reasoning versions (o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1, a Gemini flash). The LLM uncertainty-bonus parameter phi stays negative for all LLMs on the 4-armed task. 2-armed: 20 trials of 10 rounds per agent. Humans in the 4-armed task: 1 trial of 300 or 2 of 150 rounds.
limits: Behavioural model fits, not a benchmark of final score. LLMs did not match any single algorithm.
agent_relevance: Reasoning helps but is not enough on harder multi-option problems; a code-side exploration bonus still earns its place for many operators.

source: Semantic Bandits (2026) In-Context Exploration-Exploitation is Biased by Semantic Priors
finding: Arm names change what the LLM explores. Positive-sounding labels get exploited even when reward is lower; misleading labels raise regret. Negative reward values cause far more exploration than positive ones. A warning plus an instruction to explore raises exploration; a warning alone only slightly.
numbers: Models Gemini, Qwen3, OLMo. Alphanumeric labels behave close to a UCB baseline. The reward-sign effect is stronger for Qwen3 and OLMo than for Gemini. Reward magnitude effect non-monotonic and inconsistent.
limits: Numbers mostly in figures; I read only the text. The warning increased regret when labels were helpful.
agent_relevance: If an LLM sees operator names, its choice is biased by their wording. Use neutral ids when the model must choose, and prefer a code-side choice.

source: Berdica et al. (2026) When Do We Need LLMs? A Diagnostic for Language-Driven Bandits
finding: In contextual bandits with text, lightweight numeric bandits on text embeddings often match or beat LLM-based agents. LLM bandits win only when the reward function is complex and non-linear. When the reward is linear, LinUCB converges fastest and LLM methods do worse.
numbers: Compared LinUCB and other numeric contextual bandits with LLMP-UCB and LLMP-Joint on synthetic reward functions (nonlin1, nonlin2, linear, LLM-defined) and Banking77.
limits: Synthetic rewards; figure numbers not read.
agent_relevance: An LLM as selector must beat a cheap numeric bandit to be worth its tokens. Default to the cheap one.

source: Hu et al. (2024-2025) PAK-UCB Contextual Bandit: Prompt-Aware Selection of Generative Models and LLMs
finding: Routes each prompt to the better model using a kernel-based contextual UCB, with a random-feature speedup. The online learner can beat the single best-on-average model when models are better on different prompt types.
numbers: Regret bound O~(sqrt(G T)) for the RFF version. Sudoku: o3-mini 70.82% vs DeepSeek-Chat 50.42% on boards with more than 15 blanks, but 86.85% vs 93.6% on easier boards. HumanEval: Gemini-2.5-Flash 92.3% vs 86.5% on Python completion; 48.8% vs 82.3% on Java-to-C++.
limits: Two-model pools; context is a text embedding; results in figures.
agent_relevance: Operator value depends on problem type, so average rankings mislead. Context (problem class) must enter selection.

source: TI-UCB authors (2024) Which LLM to Play? Convergence-Aware Online Model Selection with Time-Increasing Bandits
finding: Arms whose reward rises as they are used (a model being fine-tuned) break standard bandits. TI-UCB fits a rising trend and detects when it levels off. Regret bound O(log T / Delta_min^2). Sliding-window UCB converges to a suboptimal arm and gets linear regret.
numbers: Synthetic: 200,000 steps with 2 arms and 1,500,000 steps with 15 arms. LLM test: GPT-3 Davinci vs GPT-2 Medium and T5 Base on summarisation, reward includes fine-tuning cost; small models overtake Davinci after some steps. Change window 16 to 2048 steps works on IMDB, 2 to 128 on LLM bandits.
limits: Needs thousands of pulls; not a small-budget method.
agent_relevance: Warns that an operator's payoff can change as the state moves, but gives no tool for runs of a few dozen pulls.

source: TextBandit authors (2025) TextBandit: Evaluating Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs Through Language-Only Decision Tasks
finding: Bandits with only text feedback ('you earned a token'). One small model hit an 89.2% best-arm rate; three others were below the Thompson and UCB baselines. More arms made all models worse. Larger was not better.
numbers: 500 runs of 25 rounds; arms 2 to 5; best arm has 65% success. Best-arm rate: Qwen3-4B 89.2%, Qwen3-8B 37.5%, Llama-3.1-8B 31.6%, Phi-2 25.4%; Thompson 51.1%, UCB 47.6%, epsilon-greedy 38.1%, random 31.8%. Llama-3.1-8B fell from 31.56% (2 arms) to 7.37% (5 arms).
limits: Small-lab study, 25 rounds. The Qwen3-4B figure is one outlier model; the 4B-over-8B ordering is unexplained and may be a prompt or format quirk. Not replicated in other work I read.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on one model's lucky bandit behaviour. Arm count hurts: keep the live operator set small.

source: DaCosta, Fialho, Schoenauer, Sebag (2008) Adaptive Operator Selection with Dynamic Multi-Armed Bandits, GECCO
finding: The classic non-LLM system. D-MAB restarts UCB1 when a Page-Hinkley test sees a change in rewards. Compared with Probability Matching and Adaptive Pursuit on a switching-operator scenario, the bandit methods win. Static scaled MAB wins on the Boolean scenario; D-MAB wins when changes are frequent or rare depending on scaling.
numbers: 5 operators, epochs T = 50 and T = 200, 3 reward scenarios (uniform, Boolean, outlier), 100 runs per setting, 1-way ANOVA at 95%. Best p_min for Probability Matching and Adaptive Pursuit was 0 to 0.01, not the 0.1 of the original paper. Restart worked better than discounting.
limits: Artificial reward sequences, not real evolutionary runs. D-MAB adds two parameters (threshold, delta).
agent_relevance: Restart-on-change is the proven way to handle a shifting best operator; our detector can be a code-checked event such as stagnation. Parameter-light methods are safer.

source: Fialho et al. (2008-2010) Extreme value credit assignment and Extreme Compass with D-MAB
finding: From a search summary: rewards based on the largest recent gain, not the average gain, handled rare big wins in evolutionary operator selection. Combined with D-MAB this gave good results on SAT instances.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened this session. Verify before use.
agent_relevance: Credit assignment by maximum gain over a window matches ShinkaEvolve's exponential reward; both favour bold operators.

source: RIDER (FRUCT proceedings, vol 39) Windowed Thompson Sampling over nine evolutionary prompt operators
finding: From a search summary: windowed Thompson sampling with an epsilon-greedy overlay over nine prompt operators in an LLM evolutionary loop.
numbers: Not read; the PDF download was damaged.
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Another LLM-loop use of windowed Thompson sampling; check later.

source: BRACIS (2021) Online Selection of Heuristic Operators with Deep Q-Network: HyFlex study
finding: From a search summary: a DQN selector beat two bandit selectors on instances where more exploitation helped, across six HyFlex domains.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. Summary level only.
agent_relevance: Hyper-heuristic evidence that a learned state-conditioned selector can beat a context-free bandit when a good state is available.
